glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 30 records the words of Agur, who confesses that he cannot reach the knowledge of the Holy One alone, asks the name of God’s Son, rests on God’s pure word, and teaches humility through numbered sayings drawn from life and creation.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Agur the son of Jakeh is otherwise unknown, and the book presents him as a wise man distinct from Solomon. His words follow the proverbs copied by Hezekiah’s men (25:1) and precede King Lemuel’s (31:1).

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Every word of God is pure; He is a shield to those who put their trust in Him.” (Proverbs 30:5)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Agur begins where most teachers would end, with what he does not know: “I neither learned wisdom Nor have knowledge of the Holy One” (30:3). His confession is the fear of the LORD at work, a right view of God that sees how far the Creator stands above human reach. He presses the point with questions only the Creator can answer, and ends, “What is His name, and what is His Son’s name, If you know?” (30:4). Agur leaves the name unspoken. The answer comes in Jesus: “No one has ascended to heaven but He who came down from heaven, that is, the Son of Man” (John 3:13).

Unable to climb to heaven, Agur stands on what God has spoken, “Every word of God is pure” (30:5), and asks only for truth and daily bread (30:8). He then counts what he sees in threes and fours: a generation pure in its own eyes, appetites that never say “Enough!”, and small creatures that are exceedingly wise. Among the wonders is “the way of a man with a virgin” (30:19), set beside an adulterous woman who says, “I have done no wickedness” (30:20). Read in light of Christ and His Bride (Ephesians 5:32), faithful love and its counterfeit stand side by side, just before the book’s closing portrait of a virtuous wife.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 30:1–4 — Agur’s Confession and His Question

Agur opens with a confession instead of confident instruction, admitting that he lacks understanding and the knowledge of the Holy One, and that humility is where his wisdom begins. He then asks who has gone up to heaven and rules the wind, the waters, and the ends of the earth, and what the name of that One and of His Son might be, a question answered in Jesus, the Son of Man who came down from heaven (John 3:13).

Proverbs 30:5–6 — Every Word of God Is Pure

Over against his own limits Agur sets the reliability of God, whose every word is tested and true and who shields those who trust Him. Because His words are pure, anyone who adds his own ideas to them invites God’s rebuke and is exposed as a liar (compare Deuteronomy 4:2).

Proverbs 30:7–9 — Neither Poverty nor Riches

Agur asks God for two things before he dies: a life kept far from falsehood, and the food allotted to him each day without poverty or riches. He knows that fullness can lead a man to say “Who is the LORD?” and that want can tempt him to steal, so he asks to stay faithful between the two.

Proverbs 30:10–14 — A Generation That Curses and Devours

A warning not to slander a servant to his master, since even the lowly have a just cause before God, leads into four portraits of a corrupt generation. It curses its parents, counts itself clean while still unwashed, looks down on everyone with lofty eyes, and ends by devouring the poor with teeth like swords.

Proverbs 30:15–17 — Things Never Satisfied

The leech’s two daughters, crying “Give and Give!”, introduce four things that never say “Enough!”: the grave, the barren womb, the thirsty earth, and fire, though the barren womb pictures unfulfilled longing rather than greed. The section returns to the generation of 30:11 with a grim warning that the eye that mocks father and mother will meet a shameful, unburied end.

Proverbs 30:18–20 — Four Ways Too Wonderful and the Adulterous Woman

Agur marvels at four ways that leave no trail: an eagle in the air, a serpent on a rock, a ship at sea, and the love of a man and a young woman. As a layered, spiritual reading they picture the ascension of Christ or the Spirit’s movement, Satan finding no foothold on Christ the Rock (John 14:30), the Church carried through the world by the Spirit, and Christ with His Bride (Ephesians 5:32), while the adulterous woman who wipes her mouth and denies any wrong is the counterfeit of faithful love.

Proverbs 30:21–23 — Four Things the Earth Cannot Bear

The earth trembles under four reversals: a servant suddenly made king, a fool filled with food, a hateful woman who gets married, and a maidservant who takes her mistress’s place. The danger lies in the sudden upheaval and the character carried into it, for a wise servant can rule well (17:2).

Proverbs 30:24–28 — Four Small but Wise Creatures

Ants, rock badgers, locusts, and the spider are little on the earth yet exceedingly wise. Each teaches a plain kind of wisdom that does not depend on strength: preparing in summer, taking shelter in the crags, advancing together in order, and holding on until it reaches a king’s palace.

Proverbs 30:29–31 — Four Things Stately in Walk

The last numerical saying turns to four that move with dignity: the lion that turns away from nothing, the greyhound, the male goat, and a king with his troops around him. The list climbs to the king, whose bearing is most stately when his army stands with him.

Proverbs 30:32–33 — Put Your Hand on Your Mouth

Anyone who has foolishly exalted himself or plotted evil is told to put his hand over his mouth before pride does more harm. As churning brings butter and wringing the nose brings blood, pressing anger always ends in strife.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 30 keeps the book’s practical wisdom from becoming self-confidence. Agur’s honest confession shows that the way into wisdom starts with admitting how little anyone knows of God unaided, and his question about God’s Son points past Proverbs to the One who came down from heaven to make the Father known.

Agur also guards the way God’s word is handled. Because every word of God is pure, no one may add to it, so even faithful interpretation must never be passed off as Scripture itself (30:6). His prayer for neither poverty nor riches (30:8–9) names plainly what many forget, that plenty and want can each pull a heart away from God.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Humility before the Holy One. Agur confesses his limits at the start and tells the proud to cover their mouths at the end, framing the chapter with humility (30:2–3, 32).

God’s pure word. Every word of God is pure, and He is a shield to those who trust Him; nothing is to be added to His words (30:5–6).

Enough and never enough. Agur asks for the food allotted to him (30:8–9), while the leech’s daughters, the grave, and the fire never say “Enough!” (30:15–16).

Pride and contempt. A generation that curses its parents, thinks itself clean, and looks down on others ends by devouring the poor, and the eye that mocks a father comes to a shameful end (30:11–14, 17).

Wonder at God’s world. Agur studies eagles and ships, ants and locusts, lions and kings, and finds lessons and mysteries in each (30:18–19, 24–31).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Agur the son of Jakeh (30:1). A wise man known only from this chapter and distinct from Solomon. The NKJV calls his words an “utterance” (30:1).

The Holy One (30:3). A name for God that stresses His holiness, His being unlike any other. Agur’s admission that he lacks this knowledge is itself the right view of God with which wisdom begins (9:10).

Three things, yes four (30:15, 18, 21, 29). A numerical pattern that groups observations and lands on the last item for emphasis, as in 6:16. It is not meant to set three against four.

Virgin (30:19). A young woman of marriageable age. The Hebrew word (’almah) is the one used in Isaiah 7:14, and in the natural sense Agur marvels at the mystery of love between a man and a young woman.

The adulterous woman (30:20). She “eats and wipes her mouth,” treating sin as lightly as a finished meal, and denies any wrong. Placed beside the man and the virgin, she is the counterfeit of faithful love, as the harlot stands against the Bride.

Put your hand on your mouth (30:32). A gesture of silence before God or others, as when Job said, “I lay my hand over my mouth” (Job 40:4). Agur’s closing counsel brings the chapter back to the humility with which it opened.

focus: Proverbs 30 records the words of Agur, who confesses the limits of human wisdom, asks the name of God and His Son, rests on the purity of God’s word, and prays for neither poverty nor riches, followed by numerical sayings drawn from human life and creation.

sections.title: Agur’s Confession and His Question
sections.summary: Agur confesses that he lacks understanding and the knowledge of the Holy One, and asks who has ascended into heaven and gathered the wind, and what is His name and His Son’s name.

sections.title: Every Word of God Is Pure
sections.summary: Every word of God is pure, and He is a shield to those who trust Him; no one is to add to His words.

sections.title: Neither Poverty nor Riches
sections.summary: Agur asks God to remove falsehood from him and give him neither poverty nor riches, lest he be full and deny the LORD or be poor and steal.

sections.title: A Generation That Curses and Devours
sections.summary: A servant is not to be maligned. Agur describes a generation that curses its parents, is pure in its own eyes, looks down in pride, and devours the poor.

sections.title: Things Never Satisfied
sections.summary: The leech’s daughters cry give, and the grave, the barren womb, the dry earth, and fire are never satisfied. The eye that mocks a father will be food for the ravens.

sections.title: Four Ways Too Wonderful and the Adulterous Woman
sections.summary: The way of an eagle, a serpent, a ship, and a man with a virgin are too wonderful to understand. Beside them stands the way of the adulterous woman, who says she has done no wrong.

sections.title: Four Things the Earth Cannot Bear
sections.summary: The earth cannot bear a servant who reigns, a fool filled with food, a hateful woman married, or a maidservant who replaces her mistress.

sections.title: Four Small but Wise Creatures
sections.summary: The ants, rock badgers, locusts, and spider are small but exceedingly wise in preparing, sheltering, advancing together, and reaching kings’ palaces.

sections.title: Four Things Stately in Walk
sections.summary: The lion, the greyhound, the male goat, and a king with his troops are stately in their bearing.

sections.title: Put Your Hand on Your Mouth
sections.summary: Whoever has exalted himself foolishly or devised evil should put his hand on his mouth, for the forcing of wrath produces strife.

1.brief: The chapter records the words of Agur the son of Jakeh, a wise man otherwise unknown, given as his utterance to Ithiel and Ucal. A new voice now speaks, distinct from Solomon’s, and he begins with a confession instead of confident instruction.
1.explain:
“The words of Agur the son of Jakeh,”

A new heading opens the chapter and a new voice speaks. Agur the son of Jakeh is otherwise unknown; Scripture names him only here and gives no family history beyond his father’s name. He is presented as his own author, distinct from Solomon, whose proverbs ended at 29:27. God did not need a famous name to give His people wisdom, and Agur’s words stand in the book beside the king’s.

“his utterance.”

The NKJV calls Agur’s words an “utterance,” a solemn and weighty saying. The term marks what follows as serious speech meant to be heard and received, not casual opinion.

“This man declared to Ithiel—to Ithiel and Ucal:”

“This man declared” introduces Agur’s formal address. Read as the NKJV gives it, Ithiel and Ucal are the people to whom he spoke, perhaps his students or sons, and the repetition of Ithiel’s name gives the line a personal, earnest tone. Wisdom in Proverbs is always passed on to someone. What Agur declares will begin, surprisingly, with a confession of his own limits rather than confident instruction.
1.notes:
The Hebrew word behind “utterance” is often translated oracle or burden, a weighty message. The ESV and NASB read “oracle,” and the KJV “prophecy.” Some take the word instead as the name of a people or region, Massa, which appears among the sons of Ishmael in Genesis 25:14. The same word stands in the heading of Lemuel’s words at 31:1.

The names Ithiel and Ucal are also debated. By dividing the Hebrew letters differently, some read the line as a lament, and the ESV and NLT render it, “I am weary, O God,” continuing with words about being worn out. The NKJV, NASB, and KJV keep both names. The current NIV (2011) keeps Ithiel and then reads the rest as a lament about weariness, noting in its footnote that this follows a different division of the Hebrew words.

The medieval Jewish commentator Rashi identified Agur with Solomon, explaining the name as the one who gathered understanding and saying that the Sages read it this way. The text itself gives no such identification, and the heading presents Agur’s words as a separate collection.

2.brief: Agur declares himself more stupid than any man, lacking even ordinary human understanding. His words are the honest humility of a man who has measured himself against God, and that humility is where his wisdom begins.
2.explain:
“Surely I am more stupid than any man,”

Agur opens with a startling confession. “Stupid” is a strong word, used in Proverbs of the brutish man who “hates correction” (12:1). Agur applies it to himself. He has measured himself against God and found that, by that measure, he has nothing to boast of. This is not false modesty or self-hatred; it is honesty. Wisdom begins when a person stops pretending to know what he does not know.

“And do not have the understanding of a man.”

He adds that he lacks even ordinary human understanding. The point is not that Agur was ignorant in everyday matters, for the rest of the chapter shows a keen observer of life. He is confessing that his own understanding cannot reach the things that matter most. His humility is the doorway to the questions of 30:4 and the trust of 30:5. In Proverbs, the person who knows his limits is teachable, and the teachable person grows wise.
2.notes: The KJV reads “brutish” for “stupid,” bringing out the sense of being like a beast in understanding.

3.brief: He has not learned wisdom and does not have knowledge of the Holy One. Agur admits that God cannot be reached by human effort alone, which is the right view of God that the fear of the LORD starts with.
3.explain:
“I neither learned wisdom”

Agur says he has not learned wisdom. Coming from a man whose sayings are part of Proverbs, this is not a denial that he had studied; it is a confession that wisdom in its fullness lies beyond what study alone can master. He speaks as one who knows how much remains unknown.

“Nor have knowledge of the Holy One.”

The deepest lack is knowledge of “the Holy One,” God who is unlike any other. Proverbs has already said, “the knowledge of the Holy One is understanding” (9:10). Agur admits that this knowledge cannot be reached by human effort. God is known only as He makes Himself known. This admission is itself the right view of God with which the fear of the LORD begins: God is high and holy, and people are dependent on Him. Agur’s confession does not express doubt or unbelief. It is the posture of a man who reverences God too much to claim that he has grasped Him.
3.notes:
The phrase “knowledge of the Holy One” repeats the wording of 9:10, where it is paired with the fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom.

In Hebrew the verb in the second line is know, as the KJV margin notes: Agur says he does not know the knowledge of the Holy One.

4.brief: Agur presses his confession with questions only the Creator can answer, about the One who rules heaven, wind, waters, and the ends of the earth. He ends, “What is His name, and what is His Son’s name, If you know?” Agur does not supply the name, but the question finds its answer in Jesus, who told Nicodemus in John 3:13 that the Son of Man had come down from heaven.
4.explain:
“Who has ascended into heaven, or descended?”

Agur presses his confession with questions only the Creator can answer. The first asks who has gone up to heaven and come back down, able to report what is there. No human being can climb into heaven by his own power and come back with full, independent knowledge of God to report. Whatever people know of heaven, they know because God has chosen to reveal it.

“Who has gathered the wind in His fists? Who has bound the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth?”

The next questions point to the Creator’s works. Only God holds the wind as if it were in His closed hands, wraps the waters as in a cloak, holding the clouds and seas in their place, and fixes the boundaries of the earth. The capital “His” in the NKJV shows that the One in view is God. These are questions that humble the questioner, much like the questions God put to Job.

“What is His name, and what is His Son’s name, If you know?”

Agur ends by asking the name of this Creator and the name of “His Son.” He does not supply the answer, and the questions leave every human reader without one. Yet the question about God’s Son finds its answer in Jesus, who told Nicodemus that “No one has ascended to heaven but He who came down from heaven, that is, the Son of Man” (John 3:13). Agur’s question does not show that he knew the Son’s name. It stands as a prophetic witness, answered when the Son came down from heaven and made the Father known.
4.notes:
Similar questions about the Creator’s works appear in God’s questions to Job (Job 38:4–11) and in Isaiah 40:12, which asks who has “measured the waters in the hollow of His hand” (Isaiah 40:12).

The ending is rendered in two ways, because the Hebrew can be read either as a question or as an exclamation. The NKJV and KJV read it as a question, while the ESV and NASB read it as an exclamation beginning “Surely,” and the NLT renders it as a challenge: “Tell me if you know!”

5.brief: Against his own limits Agur sets the reliability of God: every word of God is pure, tested and true, and He is a shield to those who trust Him. The man who cannot climb to heaven can rest on what God has spoken.
5.explain:
“Every word of God is pure;”

Against his own limits Agur sets the reliability of God. He cannot climb to heaven, but God has spoken, and “every word” He speaks is pure. The picture is of metal refined in fire until nothing false remains in it. God’s words have been tested and found true. Agur does not say most of God’s words, but every one.

“He is a shield to those who put their trust in Him.”

The line moves from God’s word to God Himself. The shield is not the word as a separate thing but God, who stands between His people and harm. Those who trust Him find Him to be their protection. David used almost the same words in his song of deliverance, “He is a shield to all who trust in Him” (Psalm 18:30). Agur’s honest uncertainty about himself finds its resting place here: he may not have the knowledge of the Holy One by his own effort, but he can rely on the Holy One’s word and take shelter in Him.
5.notes:
The Hebrew word behind “pure” means refined, the way metal is purified in a furnace until no impurity remains. The KJV margin reads “purified,” the NASB “tested,” and the ESV and NLT “proves true.” Psalm 12:6 uses the same picture: “The words of the LORD are pure words, Like silver tried in a furnace of earth” (Psalm 12:6).

The verse closely matches Psalm 18:30 and 2 Samuel 22:31, which also join the tested word of the LORD with the LORD as a shield to all who trust in Him.

6.brief: Because God’s words are pure, no one should add to them, or God will rebuke him and expose him as a liar. Human ideas must never be passed off as God’s word (compare Deuteronomy 4:2).
6.explain:
“Do not add to His words,”

Because God’s words are pure, nothing needs to be mixed into them. Adding to them corrupts what was perfect. Moses gave the same warning to Israel: “You shall not add to the word which I command you, nor take from it” (Deuteronomy 4:2). Human ideas, traditions, and claims must never be passed off as what God has said. This warning applies to every teacher and every study of Scripture, including this one: careful interpretation remains interpretation and must not be presented as Scripture itself.

“Lest He rebuke you, and you be found a liar.”

God Himself will rebuke the one who adds to His words. The person who claims God’s authority for his own ideas will be exposed for what he is, a liar. The warning is especially serious for anyone who says, “God says,” about something God has not said. It calls for humility and care whenever God’s word is taught or applied.
6.notes: The word for “liar” here comes from the same Hebrew root as “lies” in 30:8, where Agur asks God to keep lies far from him.

7.brief: Turning now to prayer, Agur asks God for two things and pleads not to be refused before he dies. His humility leads him to ask, and he wants these requests answered for the whole of his life.
7.explain:
“Two things I request of You”

Agur turns from confession and declaration to prayer, speaking directly to God. His humility leads him to ask. He names a number before he names the requests, a habit that marks the rest of his chapter with its threes and fours. Prayer is the natural response of a man who knows his limits and trusts God’s word.

“(Deprive me not before I die):”

He pleads that God will not refuse him these two things for as long as he lives. The requests are not for a single moment of need but for the whole of his life. He wants to live and die with these gifts. The urgency shows how much Agur values what he is about to ask: a truthful heart and a life provided for in a way that keeps him faithful to God.
7.notes: The KJV reads “deny me,” and the NASB reads “refuse me,” where the NKJV has “Deprive me not.”

8.brief: He asks God to keep falsehood and lies far from him, and to give him neither poverty nor riches but only the food appointed for him each day. Agur wants a truthful life and enough to live on (compare Matthew 6:11).
8.explain:
“Remove falsehood and lies far from me;”

The first request is for truth. Falsehood here is emptiness, what is hollow and worthless, and lies are deceptive words. Agur asks God to keep both far from him, whether they come from others or from his own heart. Having just warned against adding lies to God’s words (30:6), he asks to be kept from lies himself. He knows he cannot guard his heart by his own strength, so he asks God to do it.

“Give me neither poverty nor riches—”

The second request is for a life between two extremes. Agur does not idealize poverty, and he does not seek wealth. He asks for what will keep him faithful to God, and 30:9 explains why both extremes are dangerous.

“Feed me with the food allotted to me;”

“Allotted” describes a set portion, the daily share appointed for him. Agur asks for enough: neither so little that he is driven to desperation nor so much that he forgets God. Jesus taught His disciples to pray in the same spirit, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11). Paul later wrote, “having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Timothy 6:8). Contentment with God’s provision is a form of trust in Him.
8.notes: The KJV reads “vanity” for “falsehood,” bringing out the sense of emptiness. For “the food allotted to me,” the NASB reads “my portion,” and the KJV margin gives “allowance.”

9.brief: He explains the danger at each extreme: fullness could lead him to deny God and say, “Who is the LORD?” while poverty could tempt him to steal and dishonor the name of his God. Both plenty and want can pull a heart away from God, and Agur prays to stay faithful in between.
9.explain:
“Lest I be full and deny You, And say, ‘Who is the LORD?’”

Agur explains the danger of riches first. A full person can come to feel he needs no one, not even God. Comfort quietly becomes self-sufficiency, and self-sufficiency turns into denial. “Who is the LORD?” is the question of a heart that no longer feels its dependence. Pharaoh spoke the same words in open defiance: “Who is the LORD, that I should obey His voice” (Exodus 5:2). Moses warned Israel that when they had eaten and were full, their hearts could be lifted up and forget the LORD (Deuteronomy 8:12–14). Agur knows his own heart well enough to fear what plenty might do to it.

“Or lest I be poor and steal, And profane the name of my God.”

The opposite danger is poverty. Desperate need can tempt a person to steal, and a thief who belongs to God brings dishonor on God’s name. Agur is concerned for more than his own comfort. He cares how his life reflects on the God he serves. His prayer is that he will stay faithful in between, held where both his dependence on God and his honor of God’s name are kept safe. Both plenty and want can pull a heart away from God.
9.notes: The KJV renders “profane” as taking the name of God “in vain,” and its margin gives “belie thee” for “deny You.”

10.brief: Do not slander a servant to his master, or the servant will curse you and you will be found guilty. Even the lowly have a just cause before God, and running them down brings guilt on the accuser.
10.explain:
“Do not malign a servant to his master,”

To malign is to slander, to speak against someone with harmful words. A servant was in a weak position, easily accused and seldom able to defend himself before his master. Agur warns against using that weakness to bring him down with an accusation. The lowly are not fair game for careless or malicious words, and God sees how they are treated.

“Lest he curse you, and you be found guilty.”

The wronged servant may call down a curse on the accuser, and the slanderer will be found guilty. His guilt is real because his accusation was unjust, and the One who judges it is God, not the servant. Proverbs also says that “a curse without cause shall not alight” (26:2); a curse has no power of its own, and the outcome rests with the LORD. Even the lowliest person has a just cause before God. The saying stands at the head of the section that follows, where contempt and cruelty toward others, especially the weak, mark a corrupt generation.
10.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “malign” means to use the tongue against someone, that is, to slander. The KJV margin gives this literal sense: Hurt not with thy tongue. The ESV reads “slander.”

11.brief: Agur describes a generation that curses its father and refuses to bless its mother. The first of four portraits of a corrupt generation begins with contempt for parents.
11.explain:
“There is a generation that curses its father,”

These words introduce the first of four portraits of a kind of people. Here the word generation means a class or type of person rather than everyone born in a given period. This kind of person curses its father, speaking against him with contempt and wishing him harm. God’s law treated such cursing as a grave offense (Exodus 21:17), and Proverbs warns that the one who curses his parents will have his lamp put out (20:20).

“And does not bless its mother.”

The second line describes neglect rather than open attack. This generation does not bless its mother, withholding the honor, gratitude, and good words she is owed. The command to “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12) is broken both by cursing and by silent ingratitude. The portrait of a corrupt generation begins at home, with contempt for parents, and it will end in cruelty toward the poor (30:14).
11.notes: The NASB renders “generation” as “a kind,” and the ESV as “those,” showing that the word describes a type of people rather than an age group or historical period. The same opening is repeated in 30:11–14.

12.brief: Another mark of this generation is that it is pure in its own eyes yet has never been washed from its filth. Self-righteousness blinds people to the very uncleanness that most needs washing.
12.explain:
“There is a generation that is pure in its own eyes,”

The second portrait is self-righteousness. This kind of person judges himself clean by his own standard and sees no need for washing. Proverbs warns, “All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, But the LORD weighs the spirits” (16:2). Self-assessment is easily fooled.

“Yet is not washed from its filthiness.”

The truth is the opposite of the self-image. This generation is still filthy, unwashed from its sin. The word filthiness is strong, describing real defilement. The tragedy is that the uncleanness that most needs washing is hidden from those who think themselves pure. Only someone who admits he is dirty seeks to be washed. The contrast with Agur is striking: he confessed his lack before God (30:2–3), while this generation boasts of a purity it does not have.

13.brief: This generation is also proud, with lofty eyes and lifted eyelids. Its arrogance shows in the way it looks down on everyone else.
13.explain:
“There is a generation—oh, how lofty are their eyes!”

The third portrait is pride. Agur breaks into an exclamation, “oh” (30:13), as if the sight of such arrogance startles him. Lofty eyes look down on everyone. A proud look is among the things the LORD hates (6:17), and pride shows itself first in how a person looks at others.

“And their eyelids are lifted up.”

The second line paints the same picture in detail: eyelids raised in disdain, the expression of someone who holds others in contempt. The portraits are building toward a climax. Contempt for parents (30:11) and confidence in one’s own purity (30:12) grow into an arrogance that looks down on the whole world, and that arrogance prepares the way for the cruelty of 30:14.
13.notes: The NASB adds the words “in arrogance” in brackets to make the sense of raised eyelids explicit, and the NLT speaks of “disdainful” glances.

14.brief: Worst of all, this generation has teeth like swords and fangs like knives, devouring the poor from the earth and the needy from among men. Contempt for parents, self-righteousness, and pride end in cruelty toward the weakest.
14.explain:
“There is a generation whose teeth are like swords, And whose fangs are like knives,”

The fourth portrait is the worst. Agur pictures people as predators with teeth like swords and fangs like knives. Their mouths are weapons. They tear at others with their words and their schemes as a wild animal tears its prey. The picture shows how far the earlier sins can go when they are not checked.

“To devour the poor from off the earth, And the needy from among men.”

Their victims are the poor and needy, those least able to defend themselves. This generation consumes them, taking their land, wages, and livelihood until they are wiped from the earth. Contempt for parents, self-righteousness, and pride end in cruelty toward the weakest. Proverbs repeatedly shows that the LORD defends the poor, for “the LORD is the maker of them all” (22:2). Those who devour the poor set themselves against God.
14.notes:
The NASB, KJV, and AMP read “jaw teeth” for “fangs.” The ESV omits “like,” giving a stronger metaphor in which the teeth are swords.

The four portraits of 30:11–14 each begin with “There is a generation,” and they move from the home (parents) to the self (purity, pride) to society (the poor).

15.brief: The leech has two daughters, “Give and Give!” a picture of appetite that only demands more. Agur then introduces a numerical saying: three things, yes four, are never satisfied and never say, “Enough!”
15.explain:
“The leech has two daughters— Give and Give!”

Agur begins a new kind of saying with a vivid picture. The leech clings and sucks blood. Its “two daughters” are the offspring that share its nature, and their names are their only words: “Give and Give!” The picture is appetite that only demands more and is never filled. It makes a fitting bridge from the devouring generation of 30:14, whose hunger for what belongs to others is never satisfied.

“There are three things that are never satisfied, Four never say, ‘Enough!’:”

Agur now introduces a numerical saying. The pattern of three things, then four, gathers several examples and lands with emphasis on the last. It is a teaching device, not a riddle about numbers; the same pattern appears in “These six things the LORD hates, Yes, seven” (6:16). Each of the four that follow shares one trait: it never says, “Enough!”
15.notes:
The Hebrew word for “leech” occurs only here in the Old Testament; it comes from a root meaning to suck. The KJV reads “horseleach,” and the NLT interprets the two daughters as the leech’s two “suckers.”

The numerical pattern of one number followed by the next (three, then four) recurs through the chapter (30:15, 18, 21, 29), as it does in 6:16.

16.brief: The four are the grave, the barren womb, the dry earth that never has enough water, and fire that never says, “Enough!” What they share is that none of them is ever satisfied; the grave and the fire best picture the devouring generation’s appetite, while the barren womb is an unfulfilled longing, not greed.
16.explain:
“The grave, The barren womb,”

The first of the four is “the grave,” which receives the dead generation after generation and is never full. Proverbs says, “Hell and Destruction are never full” (27:20). The second is “the barren womb.” Here the picture changes character. A barren woman’s longing for a child is not greed; it is an unfulfilled longing for a good gift. Rachel cried, “Give me children, or else I die!” (Genesis 30:1), and Hannah prayed “in bitterness of soul” (1 Samuel 1:10). The barren womb belongs in the list because its longing is never quieted, not because there is anything wrong with it.

“The earth that is not satisfied with water— And the fire never says, ‘Enough!’”

The third is dry ground in a hot land, which drinks in every rain and is soon thirsty again. The fourth is fire, which consumes whatever is fed to it and always reaches for more. What the four share is that none of them is ever filled. Of the four, the grave and the fire most clearly picture the appetite of the devouring generation of 30:14, whose greed consumes without end.
16.notes:
The ESV and NASB read “Sheol” for “The grave,” the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead.

The NLT renders the third and fourth items as “the thirsty desert” and “the blazing fire,” without the repeated phrase about never saying enough.

17.brief: The eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother will be plucked out by the ravens of the valley and eaten by young eagles. The grim picture of an unburied death warns that contempt for parents ends in shame and judgment, returning to the generation of verse 11.
17.explain:
“The eye that mocks his father, And scorns obedience to his mother,”

The saying returns to the theme of 30:11, contempt for parents. The “eye” stands for the whole attitude of the person, since a mocking look often shows contempt before any word is spoken. This person mocks his father and scorns the idea of obeying his mother. His contempt is open and settled.

“The ravens of the valley will pick it out, And the young eagles will eat it.”

The punishment fits the sin: the eye that mocked will be pecked out by birds. The picture is of a body left unburied in the open, where ravens and birds of prey feed on it. In Israel such an end was a disgraceful one, the opposite of an honorable burial among one’s people. The grim image warns that contempt for parents leads to a shameful end and to judgment.
17.notes:
The ESV and NLT read “vultures” for “young eagles.” The Hebrew word covers large birds of prey, including both eagles and vultures, and vultures fit the picture of birds feeding on a corpse.

For “the valley” the KJV margin offers “the brook” as another rendering of the same Hebrew word.

18.brief: Three things, yes four, are too wonderful for Agur to understand. The man who confessed his limits in verses 2–3 now stands in wonder at mysteries in God’s world.
18.explain:
“There are three things which are too wonderful for me,”

Agur turns from appetite to wonder. Some things in God’s world are “too wonderful,” beyond his power to explain. The man who confessed his limits in 30:2–3 now stands amazed at mysteries in creation and in human life. Proverbs invites this kind of searching, for “It is the glory of God to conceal a matter” (25:2).

“Yes, four which I do not understand:”

The numerical pattern again builds to the fourth item, which is the climax of the list. Agur does not claim to solve the mysteries he names. He observes them, admits he does not understand them, and invites the reader to wonder with him. Humility before God’s works is part of wisdom.

19.brief: The four are the way of an eagle in the air, a serpent on a rock, a ship in the midst of the sea, and a man with a virgin, each passing without leaving a trail, the last being the mystery of love between a man and a young woman. As a layered, spiritual reading, the four ways picture Christ’s ascension, the tempter finding no hold on Christ the Rock, the Church carried through the world by the Spirit, and the great mystery of Christ and His Bride (Ephesians 5:32).
19.explain:
“The way of an eagle in the air,”

The four “ways” share one trait in their plain sense: each moves in a way that is hard to explain and leaves no trail behind it. The eagle rides the wind high in the sky, rising and turning without visible effort, and the air holds no track of its flight.

“The way of a serpent on a rock,”

A snake has no legs, yet it moves smoothly over bare rock. On stone it leaves no mark, and no one can follow its path afterward.

“The way of a ship in the midst of the sea,”

A ship finds its way across the open sea with no road beneath it, and its wake closes behind it so that no trace of its route remains.

“And the way of a man with a virgin.”

The last way is the climax: the mystery of love between a man and a young woman. How attraction begins, how two lives are drawn together into one, is as wonderful and untraceable as the other three. Agur does not explain it; he marvels at it as part of God’s good design.

Beyond this plain meaning, the four ways can also be read at a deeper, spiritual level that Agur does not state. As a layered reading, the eagle pictures Christ’s ascension, when “He was taken up, and a cloud received Him out of their sight” (Acts 1:9), or the unseen movement of the Spirit (John 3:8). The serpent on the rock pictures the tempter finding no foothold on Christ, the Rock (1 Corinthians 10:4), for Jesus said, “the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in Me” (John 14:30). The ship pictures the Church carried through the waters of this world by the wind of the Spirit. The man with a virgin, the summit of the four, pictures Christ and His Bride: “This is a great mystery, but I speak concerning Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32).
19.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “virgin” describes a young woman of marriageable age. It is used of Rebekah, called “the virgin” in Genesis 24:43, of Miriam, called “the maiden” in Exodus 2:8, and in Isaiah 7:14. The ESV agrees with “virgin,” and the NASB and KJV read “maid.”

In Hebrew the ship is literally in the heart of the sea, as the KJV margin notes, meaning far out in open water.

20.brief: Beside these wonders Agur sets the way of an adulterous woman, who eats, wipes her mouth, and says, “I have done no wickedness.” Her sin also leaves no visible trace, and she brushes it off as easily as wiping away a meal; set beside the man and the virgin, she is the counterfeit of faithful love, as the harlot stands against the Bride.
20.explain:
“This is the way of an adulterous woman:”

Beside the four wonders Agur sets a fifth “way,” and it is a dark one. The word “way” ties her to the list: her conduct also leaves no visible trace. After the mystery of a man with a young woman comes its corruption, the adulterous woman.

“She eats and wipes her mouth,”

The image is of someone finishing a meal and wiping her mouth clean. Her sin is treated as lightly as eating, and afterward no sign of it remains. Folly’s call in 9:17 used the same kind of picture: “Stolen water is sweet, And bread eaten in secret is pleasant” (9:17).

“And says, ‘I have done no wickedness.’”

Her final words show the deepest problem. She denies that anything wrong has happened. There is no shame, no confession, no sense of sin. Set beside the man and the virgin, she is the counterfeit of faithful love. At the layered level of 30:19, the pure mystery of Christ and His Bride stands against the harlot’s counterfeit, and this contrast prepares for the book’s closing portrait of a virtuous wife (31:10–31). The one who denies her sin cannot be cleansed from it, but “whoever confesses and forsakes them will have mercy” (28:13).
20.notes: The ESV and NASB render her last word as “wrong.” A similar denial appears in 28:24, where one who robs his parents says, “It is no transgression” (28:24).

21.brief: Under three things, yes four, the earth trembles and cannot bear up. Each is a reversal that unsettles the order of life around it.
21.explain:
“For three things the earth is perturbed,”

Agur introduces another numerical saying, this time about things that shake the order of life. “The earth is perturbed” is deliberate exaggeration: the ground itself seems to tremble under these situations. The point is that some reversals upset everyone around them, not just the people directly involved.

“Yes, for four it cannot bear up:”

The earth “cannot bear up” under them, as if they were too heavy a load. Each of the four that follow is a sudden reversal, a person placed in a position his character has not prepared him for. The trouble lies in the combination of sudden rise and unchanged character, and in the upheaval that follows.
21.notes: The ESV reads “trembles” for “is perturbed,” and the NASB “quakes.”

22.brief: The first two are a servant who becomes king and a fool who is filled with food. In that social setting a sudden rise to the throne could bring upheaval, and a well-fed fool grows more insufferable, though a servant can rule wisely (17:2), so the danger lies in the reversal, not in his station.
22.explain:
“For a servant when he reigns,”

The first is a servant who suddenly becomes king. In that social setting, a servant raised to the throne without preparation, perhaps by intrigue or revolt, could bring upheaval, using new power to settle old scores or ruling without the wisdom the position requires. Proverbs observes that it is not fitting “for a servant to rule over princes” (19:10). Yet the book also says, “A wise servant will rule over a son who causes shame” (17:2). The danger lies in the sudden reversal and the unready character, not in a servant’s station or worth.

“A fool when he is filled with food,”

The second is a fool who has plenty to eat. Comfort does not make a fool wise; it makes him more insufferable. With his needs met, he grows complacent, careless, and arrogant, and his folly has more room to do damage. Prosperity in the hands of a fool becomes a burden to everyone around him.
22.notes: The ESV and NASB read “slave” for “servant,” and “becomes king” for “reigns.”

23.brief: The last two are a hateful woman who gets married and a maidservant who displaces her mistress. A bitter spirit carries its strife into the marriage, and the maidservant’s sudden rise unsettles the whole household.
23.explain:
“A hateful woman when she is married,”

The third is a “hateful woman” who gets married. Read as the NKJV gives it, she is a bitter or odious woman who brings that spirit into the marriage, and her strife fills the home. The trouble is a sudden change of status that does not change the heart, and the home suffers for it.

“And a maidservant who succeeds her mistress.”

The fourth is a maidservant who takes her mistress’s place, whether as wife or as head of the household. Such a sudden rise could unsettle the whole house. Scripture records an example in Hagar: when she conceived by Abraham, “her mistress became despised in her eyes” (Genesis 16:4), and the household was torn by conflict. None of these sayings expresses contempt for servants or for women; they describe how sudden reversals of position, carried out without wisdom or grace, unsettle the lives of everyone involved.
23.notes:
The Hebrew word behind “hateful” means hated or unloved. The ESV and NASB read “unloved,” and the KJV “odious.” The same Hebrew word describes Leah when “the LORD saw that Leah was unloved” (Genesis 29:31).

On the reading “unloved,” the line describes a woman long rejected who suddenly gains a husband and a household. The saying names the upheaval of such a sudden change; it does not say that being unloved makes a woman bitter or unfit for marriage.

The ESV reads “displaces” for “succeeds,” and the KJV says the handmaid is “heir” to her mistress.

24.brief: Four things are little on the earth, yet they are exceedingly wise. Agur turns from what is unbearable to what is admirable, showing that wisdom does not depend on size or strength.
24.explain:
“There are four things which are little on the earth,”

Agur turns from what is unbearable to what is admirable. This time he counts four without the “three... four” pattern. His examples are small creatures, easy to overlook and weak by any ordinary measure.

“But they are exceedingly wise:”

Though little, they are “exceedingly wise.” Each displays a skill for living suited to its weakness. The lesson is plain: wisdom does not depend on size or strength. The creatures that follow teach by simple observation, as the ant did earlier: “Go to the ant, you sluggard! Consider her ways and be wise” (6:6). Agur draws practical lessons from nature without turning each creature into a hidden symbol.
24.notes: In Hebrew “exceedingly wise” is literally wise, made wise, as the KJV margin notes. The doubled wording strengthens the description, and the second word is passive, describing a wisdom the creatures have been given rather than one they achieved.

25.brief: Ants are not a strong people, yet they store up their food in summer. Their wisdom is foresight, preparing in the season of plenty for the time of need (compare 6:6–8).
25.explain:
“The ants are a people not strong,”

Agur calls the ants “a people,” a whole community, but a weak one. Any one ant is easily crushed.

“Yet they prepare their food in the summer;”

Their wisdom is foresight. In summer, when food is plentiful, they gather and store it for the lean months ahead. They do not wait for need to arrive before acting. Proverbs used the ant earlier to rebuke the lazy man, for she “Provides her supplies in the summer, And gathers her food in the harvest” (6:8). The lesson is to use the season of plenty to prepare for the time of need, whether in work, in money, or in the life of the soul.

26.brief: Rock badgers are a feeble folk, yet they make their homes in the crags. Their wisdom is knowing their weakness and living where they are protected.
26.explain:
“The rock badgers are a feeble folk,”

The “rock badgers” are small, furry animals that live among rocky cliffs in the land of Israel. Agur calls them “a feeble folk,” creatures with little power to defend themselves.

“Yet they make their homes in the crags;”

Their wisdom is knowing their weakness and living where they are protected. Instead of trusting their own strength, they take shelter in the clefts of the rocks. The psalmist observed the same thing: “The cliffs are a refuge for the rock badgers” (Psalm 104:18). Wisdom is not pretending to be strong but knowing where safety lies and staying there.
26.notes: The animal is the rock hyrax, which the NASB (1995) footnote describes as a small, shy, furry animal. The NLT reads “hyraxes,” and the KJV “conies.” The NASB keeps the Hebrew name, “shephanim.”

27.brief: Locusts have no king, yet they all advance in ranks. Their wisdom is order and unity, accomplishing together what none could do alone.
27.explain:
“The locusts have no king,”

Locusts have no ruler to command them, no leader to give orders. By human expectations, such a mass of creatures should be chaos.

“Yet they all advance in ranks;”

Yet they move together in order, as if organized into an army. A single locust is nothing, but together they sweep across whole regions. Their wisdom is order and unity, accomplishing together what none could do alone. The prophet Joel described a locust army in the same terms: “Every one marches in formation, And they do not break ranks” (Joel 2:7). The lesson is that disciplined cooperation can achieve great things even without a visible head to drive it.
27.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “advance in ranks” means to divide; here it pictures the locusts dividing themselves into companies as they move. The KJV margin gives gathered together instead, and the ESV and NLT read “march” in rank or formation.

28.brief: The spider grips skillfully with its hands and finds its way even into kings’ palaces. Its wisdom is a persistence that gains access to places far above its size and station.
28.explain:
“The spider skillfully grasps with its hands,”

The fourth creature is small enough to hold, yet it grips skillfully with its “hands,” clinging to walls and ceilings. It has no strength to force its way anywhere, but it holds on and climbs.

“And it is in kings’ palaces.”

This little creature ends up in the finest buildings in the land. No guard keeps it out, and no wall is too high for it. Its wisdom is persistence and skill, which gain access to places far above its size and station. The lesson is that faithful, skillful persistence can take the weak to places strength alone could not reach.
28.notes: The identity of this creature is uncertain. The NKJV and KJV read “spider,” while the ESV, NASB, and NLT read “lizard.” The ESV and NASB also take the first line to mean that the creature can be caught in the hand, so the contrast is between how easily it is taken and where it is found.

29.brief: Last come three things, yes four, that are majestic in pace and stately in their walk. The final numerical saying turns from small creatures to those that move with dignity and confidence.
29.explain:
“There are three things which are majestic in pace,”

The final numerical saying turns from small creatures to those that move with dignity and confidence. “Majestic in pace” describes a stride that carries authority. Agur has looked at what is unsatisfied, wonderful, unbearable, and wise; now he looks at what is stately.

“Yes, four which are stately in walk:”

The “three... four” pattern again builds to a climax in the last item. Each of the four walks with a bearing that commands respect. The list will rise from animals to a king, and the comparison sets up the warning of 30:32 against a false and foolish kind of self-exaltation.
29.notes: The ESV uses “stately” in both lines, with “tread” and “stride,” and the KJV speaks of things that “go well” and are “comely” in going.

30.brief: The first is the lion, mighty among the beasts, which turns away from nothing. Its stride carries the confidence of strength that fears no rival.
30.explain:
“A lion, which is mighty among beasts”

The first is the lion, mighty among the beasts. Its walk shows its strength. Throughout Scripture the lion stands for power and courage, and its stride is unhurried because it has nothing to fear.

“And does not turn away from any;”

The lion turns aside for no one. Faced with another creature, it does not retreat. Its confidence comes from real strength, not from show. Proverbs elsewhere says, “the righteous are bold as a lion” (28:1). The stateliness Agur admires is the bearing of a creature secure in its own nature. He does not draw a separate moral from each animal; the picture itself shows that a confident bearing rests on real strength.
30.notes: The ESV reads “turn back” and the NASB “retreat” for “turn away.”

31.brief: The others are the greyhound, the male goat, and a king with his troops around him. The list climbs to the king, whose bearing is most stately when his army stands with him.
31.explain:
“A greyhound, A male goat also,”

The second creature is uncertain in the Hebrew, but the NKJV takes it as a “greyhound,” a lean, swift dog that runs with grace. The third is the male goat, which leads the flock with a confident stride, out in front of the others.

“And a king whose troops are with him.”

The list climbs to its last and highest item: a king with his army around him. His bearing is most stately when his troops stand with him, for his authority is visible and backed by strength. The picture of rightful majesty prepares for the contrast of 30:32, where a person tries to exalt himself without any such standing.
31.notes:
The Hebrew name of the second animal occurs only here, and its meaning is uncertain. The word describes a creature girt in the loins, that is, with a belt drawn tight around the waist, a way of picturing a lean, trim body. The KJV margin offers “horse” as an alternative to “greyhound,” and the ESV, NASB, and NLT read “strutting rooster.”

The last line is also difficult. The KJV reads it as a king against whom there is “no rising” up, and the current NIV (2011) similarly speaks of a king secure against revolt, noting that the meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. The ESV and NASB speak of a king with his army.

32.brief: If you have been foolish enough to exalt yourself, or have plotted evil, put your hand over your mouth. Agur closes as he began, with humility: the right response to pride is to stop talking before it does more harm.
32.explain:
“If you have been foolish in exalting yourself,”

After the stately creatures and the king, Agur turns to the reader. Some people try to lift themselves up without the standing to do it, and that is folly. Self-exaltation is the opposite of the humility with which Agur began his words (30:2–3).

“Or if you have devised evil, put your hand on your mouth.”

The same counsel applies to anyone who has been plotting harm. “Put your hand on your mouth” means stop talking, now, before the boasting or scheming goes further. It is a gesture of silence and shame. Job used the same gesture when he stood before the LORD: “I lay my hand over my mouth” (Job 40:4). Agur closes as he began, with humility. The right response to pride and evil intentions is not to defend them but to fall silent before God and others, so that the harm stops before it grows.
32.notes: The NLT interprets “put your hand on your mouth” as covering the mouth in shame.

33.brief: As churning milk produces butter and wringing the nose produces blood, so forcing anger produces strife. Pressure applied always yields its result, and the chapter ends with a warning to stop pressing before wrath turns into open conflict.
33.explain:
“For as the churning of milk produces butter,”

Agur explains his warning with three pictures of pressure. When milk is churned or pressed, butter or curds come out. Pressing always produces its result.

“And wringing the nose produces blood,”

Squeeze or twist a nose hard enough, and blood flows. The same action produces a painful result.

“So the forcing of wrath produces strife.”

The third picture is the point. When anger is pressed and pushed, by stirring it up in oneself or provoking it in others, strife is the inevitable result. Pride and scheming, if they are not stopped (30:32), lead to angry words, and angry words pressed further lead to open conflict. The chapter ends with practical counsel: stop pressing before wrath becomes a quarrel. Agur’s words, which began with humility before God, end with humility before people.
33.notes:
The Hebrew uses the same noun three times, a word meaning squeezing or pressing. The NKJV varies it as “churning,” “wringing,” and “forcing,” while the ESV keeps “pressing” throughout. The repetition makes the point plain: the same kind of pressure that brings butter from milk and blood from a nose brings strife out of anger.

The verse also plays on words. The Hebrew word for “nose” is also the ordinary word for anger, which was pictured in flared nostrils and hard breathing, and “wrath” in the third line is a form of the same word. In Hebrew, pressing the nose and pressing anger sound almost alike.
